title: Reading the Bible With Someone
subtitle: Five sessions that hand a new believer the skill of feeding themselves from Scripture
summary: The goal of walking someone through the Bible is not to make them need you. It is to make them able to open the book on a Monday morning with no one else in the room. This study is five sessions, one on one, with a Bible open on the table the whole time. It moves from why their own hunger matters more than your knowledge, to a simple repeatable method they can use alone, to where to start a new reader, to what to do when the text confuses them, to the turn that makes it all count, from reading the Word to doing it. By the last session the other person is meant to be leading the reading, because you have been working yourself out of a job from the start.
setting: A table with two Bibles or one shared between you. Coffee is fine. Phones down. The aim is that by session five the other person is the one turning the pages and reading first.
forWho: The disciple maker who wants the person they walk with to become able to open the Bible without them, and the new reader learning how to do it.
rhythm: Five sessions, one on one, with a Bible open the whole time and the method practiced in real time. Once a week over a meal or a coffee works well.
leaderNote: The aim here is not to impress anyone with how much you know. It is to work yourself out of a job. Teach a method plain enough that the other person will actually use it alone on Monday, and let them do the reading out loud from the very first session. If you find yourself talking more than they read, you have drifted back into being the expert. Hand the book across the table. A reader who can feed themselves outlasts a teacher who made every meal for them.

sessions.title: The Goal Is Their Own Hunger
sessions.bigIdea: The point of reading together is to make the other person hungry for the Word itself, not dependent on you to explain it. Jesus said we live by every word from the mouth of God, and Jeremiah ate the words as his own joy. That hunger is the thing you are trying to hand across the table.
sessions.open: Tell me honestly, before this, what has the Bible felt like to you. A closed door, a school assignment, a book other people seem to get, or something you have never really tried to open. No wrong answer.
sessions.read: Read Jeremiah 15:16 out loud, and you read it first this time. Your words were found, and I ate them, and your words became to me a joy and the delight of my heart, for I am called by your name, O LORD, God of hosts. Then read Matthew 4:4. But he answered, It is written, Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God.
observe: Jeremiah does not say he studied the words or filed them away. What verb does he use, and what does that picture of eating suggest about how the Word is meant to be taken in.
Jesus puts the word of God next to bread. What is he saying we would starve without, and how often do people eat.
talk: I want to say this plainly on the first day. My job is not to be the person you come to whenever you have a question about the Bible. My job is to make you someone who can open it and be fed without me in the room. Does that surprise you, and does it feel like freedom or like being left alone.
Jeremiah found the words a joy, but plenty of people find the Bible a chore. Where has it felt like a chore to you, and what do you think has been missing when it did.
If reading Scripture became as normal for you as eating, not perfect, not daily at first, just normal, what would have to change about how you picture it. Say it out loud and we will start there.
sessions.practice: Between now and next time, open the Bible on your own just once. Read anything, five minutes, no pressure to understand it all. The habit matters more than the amount. Notice what it was like to sit with it alone, because that is the thing we are building.
sessions.send: You do not need me to stand between you and this book. You need a table, a few minutes, and the nerve to open it yourself.
sessions.passItOn: When you have read on your own even once, tell the person who is walking with you what it was like. And keep in mind, someday you will sit across a table from someone who has never opened this book, and you will hand them the same hunger you are being handed now.

sessions.title: A Simple Way In
sessions.bigIdea: A method you cannot remember is a method you will not use. So the whole thing fits in three moves. Read it. Notice what it says about God and about us. Respond in prayer. Nehemiah shows the Word read clearly so people understood, and the psalmist asks God to open his eyes. Plain and repeatable beats clever every time.
sessions.open: Have you ever tried to read the Bible and had no idea what you were supposed to be doing with it. Where did you get stuck, at the start, in the middle, or in the not knowing what it meant.
sessions.read: Your turn to read first today. Read Psalm 119:18. Open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law. Then read Nehemiah 8:8, from a day when the people had not heard the Scriptures in a long time. They read from the book, from the Law of God, clearly, and they gave the sense, so that the people understood the reading.
observe: Before the psalmist reads, he asks for something. What does he ask God to open, and what does that tell you about who does the real teaching.
In Nehemiah the leaders read the book clearly and gave the sense. What two things happen together there, and which one usually gets skipped when people read alone.
talk: Here is the whole method, and it fits on one hand. First, read it, out loud is best. Second, ask two questions, what does this say about God and what does this say about us. Third, turn what you found into a short prayer. That is it. Let us do it right now with the psalm we just read. You start.
The psalmist asks God to open his eyes before he reads a single line. Why does starting with that prayer change how you come to the text, instead of leaning on being smart enough to crack it.
Which of the three moves feels easy to you and which feels hard. Be honest, because the hard one is the one you will be tempted to drop when you are on your own.
sessions.practice: Three times this week, run the method on your own. Read a short passage, ask what it says about God and about us, and pray it back in a sentence or two. Same three moves every time. You are teaching your hands to do this without thinking.
sessions.send: You now have a way in that fits on one hand. Read it, notice God and notice us, pray it back. Simple enough to use on the worst morning of your week.
sessions.passItOn: The day you can run these three moves without looking, you can teach them to someone else in five minutes. Write the three steps on a card and give it away to one person who has told you the Bible feels like a locked room.

sessions.title: Where to Start Them
sessions.bigIdea: You do not hand a first grader a physics book, and you do not start a new reader in the hard letters or the middle of the law. You start with a Gospel, John or Mark, where the whole point is written down for you. John says these things were written so that you may believe. Begin where the aim is plain.
sessions.open: If a friend told you they wanted to read the Bible for the first time and asked where to begin, what would you have said a month ago. Most people guess page one, Genesis, and quietly quit around the middle of the desert.
sessions.read: Read John 20:30-31 out loud, and you lead. Now Jesus did many other signs in the presence of the disciples, which are not written in this book. But these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name.
observe: John tells you flat out why he wrote his book. What is the reason he gives, and how does knowing the aim before you read change the way you read.
The verse says these are written so that you may believe and have life. Who is the writer picturing on the other end of the page, a scholar or someone deciding whether to trust Jesus.
talk: Here is the practical counsel, and it will save you months. Start in a Gospel, John or Mark, before you go anywhere near the hard letters or the front of the Old Testament. Why do you think meeting Jesus in the story first would make the rest of the Bible make more sense later.

John wrote his whole book so that you may believe. If that is the target, how should it shape what you are looking for as you read, not first can I master this, but who is this Jesus and can I trust him.
Let us pick your starting place right now, together. John or Mark. Read the first chapter with me before you leave, using the three moves from last week, and you go first.
sessions.practice: Read one chapter of the Gospel you chose every few days this week, using the three moves. Do not rush to finish the book. Meet the person in it. Bring one thing that struck you about Jesus to our next time together.
sessions.send: You do not start a new reader in the deep end. You start them face to face with Jesus, where the whole book was aimed all along.
sessions.passItOn: When you have read a Gospel through, you will know exactly where to send the next new reader you meet, because you will have walked the road yourself. Tell one person which Gospel you started with and why you would point them there too.

sessions.title: When It Is Confusing
sessions.bigIdea: Even Peter said some of what Paul wrote is hard to understand, so a new reader hitting a wall is not a failure, it is company. The answer is context, patience, and the freedom to not understand everything at once. Jesus himself opened the disciples minds to understand, which means understanding is a gift you can ask for, not a test you pass alone.
sessions.open: You have been reading on your own now. Where did you hit something that made no sense, or made you feel like maybe this is not for people like you. Tell me the exact spot.
sessions.read: You read first. 2 Peter 3:15-16. And count the patience of our Lord as salvation, just as our beloved brother Paul also wrote to you according to the wisdom given him, as he does in all his letters when he speaks in them of these matters. There are some things in them that are hard to understand, which the ignorant and unstable twist to their own destruction, as they do the other Scriptures. Then read Luke 24:45. Then he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures.
observe: Peter, who walked with Jesus for years, admits something about Pauls letters. What does he admit, and how does that land for a brand new reader who feels lost.
In Luke, who does the opening of the mind, and who receives it. What does that tell you about where understanding finally comes from.
talk: I want you to hear this from me directly. When a page confuses you, you have not failed and you are not too dumb for this. Peter said some of it is hard, and he was there. What would change for you if you gave yourself permission to leave a hard verse unsolved for now and keep reading.

Three tools help when it is confusing. Context, read what comes before and after instead of one lonely verse. Patience, some things open on the fifth read, not the first. And prayer, because Jesus opened their minds, we do not force the lock. Which of those three do you most need to start using.

The verses also warn that people twist Scripture to their own ends. How does reading a passage in its context, and not just grabbing one line, protect you from being led somewhere the text never went.
sessions.practice: This week, when you hit something confusing, do three things. Read the paragraph around it, not just the verse. Write the question down and keep going. And ask God to open your mind before you read. Bring your written questions to me next time, and we will look at them together.
sessions.send: Confusion is not the door closing. It is the invitation to read slower, read wider, and ask the one who opens minds to open yours.
sessions.passItOn: The questions that stumped you this week are the very ones the next new reader will hit too. Keep your list. Someday it becomes the map you hand to someone else so they do not think they are the only one who got lost.

sessions.title: From Reading to Obeying
sessions.bigIdea: James says the man who hears the word and does nothing is like a man who looks in a mirror and walks away forgetting his own face. The Word was never meant to be only studied. It was meant to be done. A reader who obeys is the whole aim, and that is the reader you are becoming and the one you will help make next.
sessions.open: Think back over these weeks. Has there been a line you read that you knew, right away, was asking you to actually change something. Did you do it, put it off, or hope it would fade. Be honest, I have done all three.
sessions.read: You lead the reading, all the way through. James 1:22-25. But be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves. For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man who looks intently at his natural face in a mirror. For he looks at himself and goes away and at once forgets what he was like. But the one who looks into the perfect law, the law of liberty, and perseveres, being no hearer who forgets but a doer who acts, he will be blessed in his doing.
observe: James gives a picture of a man and a mirror. What does the man do wrong, and what is the point of looking in a mirror if you forget your face the moment you turn away.
The passage promises a blessing, but not to the one who reads. To whom, exactly, and what is the person actually doing when the blessing comes.
talk: Here is the whole method finally landing. Read it, notice God and notice us, pray it back, and then do the thing it showed you. Without that last move, all the reading is a man staring in a mirror and forgetting his own face. Where is a place, this week, the Word has been asking you to act and you have kept it at the level of reading.
James calls it the law of liberty, freedom, not a cage. How is obeying what you read a kind of freedom rather than a burden. Where have you tasted that already.

You have carried the reading all the way today. That is on purpose. You are ready to feed yourself now, and I am not going to hover. What is your plan for reading and obeying once these five sessions end and it is just you and the open book.
sessions.practice: Take one thing the Word has shown you and do it this week, an apology owed, a habit to drop, a person to forgive, a step of obedience you have been reading past. One act, not a list. Then keep the three moves going on your own. You can feed yourself now.
sessions.send: The book was never for staring at. It was for doing. Go be a doer, and be the one who is blessed in the doing.
sessions.passItOn: You started these weeks unable to open the book alone. You end them able to read, understand, and obey it on your own. That is exactly what you now hand to the next person. Find one, sit down at a table, open the book, and let them read first.
